conclusion.measured: The worker did not hang in loading. The only reader of its pipe - the runner's thread - stopped reading because it was blocked writing a 64,423-byte chunk to the notebook's raw stdout, which took nothing more after 123,075 bytes of this stage. The pipe filled, the worker blocked writing its progress bar, and the driver waited for a ready line the worker could not reach.
conclusion.reproduced: without a model, on a laptop: the same reader against a display nobody reads deadlocks the same way (tests/test_kernel_gates.py, TestAStalledDisplay.test_deadlocked_the_old_reader), and the reader it held back had taken about one chunk more than the display.
conclusion.not_established: Why the notebook's raw stdout stopped taking data in this stage after carrying 640 KB earlier. print() output kept arriving, so what stalled is the raw-descriptor path - ipykernel's descriptor capture or whatever drains the kernel's own stdout - not the notebook's message channel. Unexplained.
conclusion.consistent_with_but_not_shown_for: the main kernel's v1 and v2, whose worker wrote straight into the notebook's stderr and went silent within a second of its progress bar starting - v2's faulthandler dumps, written to the same stream, never appeared. They kept no tee, so this is inference.
conclusion.retracted: The hypothesis behind 312b757 - a process surviving SIGKILL, or the final wait hanging. This run shows neither. The bounded wait stays, as correct, but it explains nothing here.

fix: run_bounded's reader now writes only to a file; the display is drawn by its own thread from a bounded queue that drops instead of waiting; the waiting thread never writes to the display; every notebook subprocess has its output captured; and the notebook runs the same fake-worker job on its own display before downloading anything (scripts/runner_check.py)
